As interposers and substrates approach their scaling limits, 2.5D packaging is moving toward 3.5D, with tighter D2D pitch, higher bandwidth density, and lower energy per bit to overcome reticle-driven constraints on lateral scaling.

Higher integration density makes yield increasingly critical to economics. Final yield compounds across process steps, so losses at any stage directly affect overall yield.

More HBM stacks, chiplets, substrates, and bonding interfaces increase integration complexity, while some defects are detected only late in the process flow. This tightens process-control requirements across the integration flow and increases the importance of advanced inspection.

I spent a decent amount of time with Gemini 4 before launch. Overall, Gemini 4 is a big jump over previous Gemini models and it is the first non-OpenAI/Anthropic model to pass the Fable/Mythos/Astra bar. It is also much more pleasant and more agentic then previous Gemini models, without the weird personality issues that you often found in Gemini 3 series models. In fact, a big advantage is that has a very different personality and sense of taste than Claude or Astra, making it a good addition to the AI world. 

On the usefulness side, in some areas it is at least at par with OpenAI and Anthropic (it is quite creative and a good writer), but in others it lags, including at complex multi-agent work. It has a tendency to be too certain about its conclusions and a little lazy, issues not helped by the Antigravity harness not being quite as good as the competition. Still, I expect to see rapid improvements in model abilities using Gemini 4 as a base.

Here is a fun example:  "create the ultimate brutalist city builder. you should have lots of controls over buildings in ways that are delightful and inuitive to people who just want to play, but are sophisticated and deep for people who know something about architecture. you should be able to play a lot with design and approach. there should be simulation modes and different ways to view or experience the city. make it stunning. i want to host this on netlify in the end"

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said investors trade more on what they think the Fed will do than on what it should do, a view that sits uneasily with Kevin Warsh's push to say less about the outlook in pursuit of a purer market signal. 

"Having been on the market side of things for three decades, I think that what markets are looking for is they're looking for any guidance as to where the Fed is going to go. I know that bankers, investment professionals, their number one goal is to produce returns for themselves and their clients. That's their goal, that's the job. And to do that, they both want to look at what the fundamentals of the economy are doing and what they're saying, but I think they respond more based on what they think the Fed will do rather than what they think we should do. And so I think that it's important to take signal back from the markets about how the economy is progressing, but I take more signal about how the economy is progressing from the data, from the stories I hear in the district."

Election Day is 3 weeks away. As of today, early voting has begun in 15 states. Here are 5 things to know to get you ready for a vote that "could change party control of Congress, and with it, the direction of U.S. politics," according to expert @JamesMLindsay: 

1. We already know the winners of 90% of House races and 75% of Senate races, Lindsay notes. Election forecasters rank only about 20 House and just 5 Senate races as toss-ups. “In short, most congressional general elections are uncompetitive, hardly the sign of a healthy, well-functioning democracy,” writes Lindsay.

2. Control of the House of Representatives is the Democrats’ to lose, Lindsay says. "House midterms generally go badly for members of the president’s party. . . . In 2026, the Democrats need a net gain of just 3 seats to retake control of the House. With President Donald Trump’s approval number in the mid-thirties, history suggests that Democrats are a shoe-in to retake control of the House come January 3."

3. A friendly electoral cycle for Senate Republicans has turned difficult. "Unlike the House, Senate midterms elections have not historically functioned as a referendum on the president . . . . Despite these favorable political winds, Trump’s unpopularity, rising fuel prices, and a general sense that life is becoming unaffordable for too many Americans have combined to put a half dozen supposedly safe Republican seats in play," Lindsay argues.

4. Neither the Democrats nor the Republicans have cemented their control of Congress in this century. "If there is one word to summarize Congress in the 21st century, it is 'turnover,'" Lindsay notes. "Party control of the House has changed 4 times since 2000, and party control of the Senate has changed 7 times . . . . Control of one if not both houses of Congress will change after the 2026 vote, a further sign of the country’s inability to forge a stable governing coalition."

5. Election Day is also about state races. "Overlooked in the discussion about the return of divided government to Washington is what will happen in the states," Lindsay writes. "Democrats are hoping that the favorable political winds they are seeing at the national level will also boost their candidates at the state level . . . . If election forecasters are right, Democrats could emerge from Election Day 2026 controlling a majority of governorships and a near majority of state legislatures."

Read Lindsay's full analysis: https://t.co/Dn5ixCA8Td
